topComment.author: @Commander_Jim
topComment.text:
Bit harsh on MK3 I think. I remember when it first hit arcades, it was massive. It was an extremely popular game. And the home release was the biggest game around. It introduced proper combos for the first time as well as stage transitions. And it had by far the tightest gameplay of the series up to that point. Also you've got to remember that some of those characters that were missing weren't classic MK characters at the time, they were new characters introduced in the previous game so most of us weren't really missing Kitana etc at the time. Scorpion was the only one I remember people being upset at not being there.

Also in regards to fatalities in the modern games, the problem is that theyre just a cinematic now and are too long. And who wants to watch the cinematic over and over. Before they were literally a finishing move that lasted a few seconds. It was a satisfying way to finish an opponent. Now its essentially a cutscene.

topComment.author: @rainey06au
topComment.text: In my mid 40's who grew up with the franchise I can't help but find it a little bit funny seeing a 20 something year old making rankings of the original trilogy. I know you can still go back and try them, but it must feel different to not have the childhood memories connected to them as they were the cutting edge fighting games at the time. After school you would head to the local newsagency to buy a mag or pocket guide with the button combo's and then study it like assignment material until you were next out in the dark back corner of the local takeaway fish and chip shop dropping your dollar coins into the arcade in the hope that you could make it to Goro and have a few people beside you to witness your greatness, especially as you were able to perform Sub Zero's spine rip along the way.. There's an emotional connection that goes way back to making these games better than they mechanically are by today's standards.

replies.author: @tselis
replies.text: As a 20 something year old I have to say I have a similar experience to you. Given that I am from a village in Greece our only entertainment was pirated games we shared with eachother through CDs or USB sticks and a massive list of arcade games emulated through Mame32. Finding Mortal Kombat 1,2 and UMK3 on that massive list and seeing people actually being hurt for the first time in my life changed me and fighting my friends made it so much fun. It was enough to pester my mother to buy me Deception, the new-ish game at the time (Armageddon was already out), and make me fall in love even more with the franchise and story. I will forever hold the original MKs dear and near to my heart for that experience and thank you for sharing yours.

replies.author: @rainey06au
replies.text: @tselis interesting story! It's funny how this game can be life changing/altering in different ways for people (not in the 'violent videogames are bad' way) but for memories, friendships they inspired along the way.  I guess for me, playing a public Mortal Kombat arcade cabinet up to MK3 was at a time where arcade cabinets far exceeded the quality of videogames you could own at home. We were playing bubble bobble, International Karate Plus, Super Hang-on, Afterburner, at home.. Then eventually the Sega Master System and other consoles got a versions of MK1 but they were never quite 'right', and the arcade editions were like seeing a bluray version of your favorite movie.
